title: The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way | Simon Jenkins
author: Simon Jenkins
categories: Immigration and asylum | UK news | Housing | Politics | Society | England | Communities
description: In other countries, local communities have a say in their futures. If the UK were truly democratic, everywhere would be a parish in control of its own fate Poor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections. And there had certainly been objections. In September, Piddington villagers declared they were fed up with Britain. Led by their parish council and on a 92% turnout, they voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK and become a “principality”. They are joined in their protest by Barnham in Suffolk, where locals have been told this week that they are to host nearly 1,000 asylum seekers. They have set their own date on a referendum to leave the UK. Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist, author and BBC broadcaster. title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
author: Polly Toynbee
categories: Inequality | Young people | Education | Politics | Society | UK news
description: From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people. Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll . That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking. description: Reasons to refuse planning permission are limited to ‘public safety’ and ‘amenity’, writes James Ward In response to your report ( Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank, 13 November ) perhaps we could start with the harbinger of high-street decline, the digital advertising screen. You know the ones, the pavement-blocking LED monoliths, with screens on both sides broadcasting six ads per minute to passersby. Even as shops have shuttered, numbers of such ad machines skyrocketed 256% between 2018 and 2025. The ads shown are invariably for global mega-corporations, further driving commerce online, and for unhealthy products such as junk food, alcohol, gambling and vapes (although the latter are to be banned from 1 June 2027). At nearly 3 metres tall and 1.24 metres wide, they contribute to pavement clutter and disrupt sightlines of historic town centres.

title: Academic integrity matters, but students shouldn’t be penalised for using AI | Letter
author: Guardian Staff
categories: Exams | A-levels | GCSEs | AI (artificial intelligence) | Schools | England | Technology | UK news | Education
description: Berthold Schoene responds after the head of Ofqual said students could be disqualified from GCSEs and A-levels if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework Is this really the best we can do: draconically penalise the young for making use of the latest cognitive resources and tools available to them ( Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat, 18 November )? Our generation has allowed the introduction of “life-altering” new technologies into every walk of life without much democratic debate, public scrutiny or governmental oversight. And now our education leaders are threatening to jeopardise young people’s career prospects for deploying these technologies within an education system that can’t cope and struggles to adapt? We all know that AI is here to stay. And importantly, it is so much more than just a cheap cheating device. Within an incredibly short space of time, it has transformed how we work, communicate, solve problems, research and learn. Surely the pedagogical response cannot simply be to devise ever more elaborate ways of preventing students from using it?

description: Ustinov Studio, Bath Elliot Cowan is scarily convincing as the budding Potus in Donald, a high-speed, three-actor comedy from the playwright behind The Lehman Trilogy His manner and actions often seeming like improbable caricature, the current US president sets a challenge for satire, any comic exaggeration likely to be trumped by reality. Mike Bartlett’s play The 47th (2022), staged between Trump’s administrations, pursued wild fantasies about the politician’s future career that were soon superseded by odder events. Ali Abbasi’s movie The Apprentice (2024) more sensibly focused on the period from 1973 to 1986 in which the New York realtor developed the behavioural and verbal tics that make him probably the most ridiculed figure in modern history, though such mockery, until the recent midterms, largely consoled detractors while being ignored by supporters. Closer to Abbasi’s approach, Donald by the Italian dramatist Stefano Massini resembles his play The Lehman Trilogy – an international hit about the banking dynasty – in being a psychological analysis played by three actors with lightning switches of character and costume. In this case, the cut-up structure reflects Massini’s seeding conceit that only about 10 minutes of any life really matter, a total of the brief sequences in which someone makes formative or destructive choices.

description: I welcome Alan Milburn’s call for schools to focus more on students’ potential beyond exams. Yet I must ask: where is the money? At 16, life should feel like a path leading to endless opportunities. That is at least the carrot dangled in front of young people to motivate them through the gruelling years of exam preparation. “Your life starts now,” their teachers all but tell them. And though for the vast majority that is true, there is a cohort who are forced to accept that the bright futures they were promised are beyond their reach. They are the nearly one million young people aged between 16 and 24 who are not in education, employment or training (Neets). Alan Milburn’s second report on the nation’s Neets places schools at the heart of the solution. It proposes that schools should be judged not only on grades but also whether pupils continue their post-16 journey into further education or work. title: Ram through datacentres no one wants and hope the AI bubble never bursts: that’s the UK’s growth plan | George Monbiot
author: George Monbiot
categories: Datacentres - UK | Technology policy | Infrastructure | Planning policy | Economic growth (GDP) | Industrial policy | UK news | AI (artificial intelligence) | Politics
description: The government doesn’t know what they are going to be used for, but that’s beside the point. Their real purpose is to sustain the share price of big tech It should have the status of an economic law: the sectors a government does most to promote in the name of growth are the sectors most likely to tank the economy. In the UK and the US, deregulation was meant to turn the financial sector into a never-ending growth machine. We have not yet fully recovered from the crash it helped cause in 2008. Fossil fuels are the most heavily subsidised sector on Earth. All that public money makes us highly vulnerable to oil price shocks, the whims of autocrats and societal collapse caused by climate breakdown. As for the great growth priority of our time – AI and datacentres – well, don’t take it from me. As Anthropic’s IPO prospectus warns , advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”. One thing we learned from the US midterm elections is that the drive to build datacentres is less a function of real commercial demand than of the need to sustain the share price of the big tech companies. After citizens across the US voted for moratoria on new datacentres, tech stocks , which have become dangerously dominant, plummeted, triggering fears of wider contagion . Whether new datacentres are required or not, we must keep building them, because confidence depends on them, and without that confidence the bubble will pop. The more you build, and the more this value dependency grows, the bigger the bubble becomes. George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

title: Andy Burnham is in danger of over-selling his big Brussels summit. What happens if he under-delivers? | Joël Reland
author: Joël Reland
categories: Brexit | European Union | Andy Burnham | Europe | Foreign policy | Politics | UK news | World news
description: In laying a trap for himself, the PM could derail his longer-term ambition of revisiting Brexit This week’s UK-EU summit may, one day, be seen as the start of the UK’s long march back towards the EU. Andy Burnham’s much-anticipated first meeting with EU chiefs in Brussels on Friday will be used to unveil a suite of detailed agreements to improve trade and economic cooperation, before the Prime Minister kickstarts his longer term “national conversation” about a much closer form of political and economic relationship with the EU. This, as Burnham signalled in a speech on Monday night , could well culminate in Labour’s next election manifesto abandoning the party’s famous red lines, and proposing an application for EU membership. For pro-Europeans, this must read like a fever dream. Just four months ago, when Burnham took office, such a bold offer on Europe from the Labour party seemed implausible. But while Burnham has certainly reinvigorated the Brexit debate, he will have to move carefully to avoid storing up trouble for himself down the road. There is a risk that Burnham will come to be seen as someone who over-promises and under-delivers on Europe – and, in doing so, halts the growing momentum around revisiting the troublesome Brexit question. description: Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confronted There are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. Voters overestimate rates of crime, for example. Many will be sceptical of politicians who say today’s streets are safer than they used to be, although that is the reality. The challenge is to find methods of persuasion that don’t belittle the experiences of people who are afraid, and don’t like to be told their fears are unfounded. But there is a different challenge that arises when the cause of public concern is a problem that doesn’t really exist. Many people are angry about “ two-tier policing ” in Britain, supposedly characterised by disproportionately severe enforcement against white people and leniency towards minorities. There is no evidence to support a systemic bias of that kind. By contrast, the data suggests an imbalance of fair treatment goes the other way. People of colour are underrepresented in the police, disproportionately targeted with stop-and-search policies and, if arrested, likelier to have force used against them. description: As a researcher for the Milburn review, I’ve seen how we’ve failed a generation – then castigated them. Britain must break this vicious cycle Mark Mon-Williams is chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Leeds and professor of psychology at Bradford Institute of Health Research Alan Milburn and Peter Fonagy have, between them, expertly diagnosed the UK’s illness. Their reviews show we don’t just have a Neet crisis. Or a school absence crisis. Or a Send crisis. We have a neglected childhood crisis that will wreck the country’s long-term prosperity if we just keep patching over these symptoms. The solution to any problem starts with understanding its causes, and Milburn and Fonagy provide a thoughtful analysis. I have worked closely with both of them, being a topic group member for Fonagy’s independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism, and supporting Milburn with data analytics. Their reviews have followed the evidence, all of which shows a system neglecting children at scale. We have decreased benefits and slashed the support provided to children: today 4.5 million children are living in poverty. When these children grow up and are diagnosed with anxiety and depression, impeding their ability to work, they are often castigated as feckless snowflakes. It is easier to do this than admit that we have failed a generation, and that this is the predictable consequence of political decisions. Mark Mon-Williams is chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Leeds and professor of psychology at Bradford Institute of Health Research

description: In today’s newsletter: Guaranteed jobs and expanded employment support sit alongside Alan Milburn’s proposals to cut benefits for some of Britain’s million young people not in education, work or training Good morning. The former health secretary, Alan Milburn, will publish his long-awaited review into the one million young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) later today. The report will propose cutting welfare for some under-25s and spending billions on a new “deal” for young people. The government is at pains to tell you that its approach to welfare is nothing like that of the Tories’: Labour isn’t the party of “crude” benefit cuts, and it sees youth worklessness as a “moral” issue for which young people aren’t to blame. It’s hard to recall a government report more heavily trailed than this one. It envisages a new relationship between young people and the state, and aims to get more young people into work and education while addressing the cost of young people becoming Neets. description: Americans are at a real point of decision – not election day, but this heady, uncertain moment after Until 2026, the most important midterm year of the last quarter-century was very probably 2010. Barack Obama famously called the elections a “shellacking” for the Democratic party and he was right. Thanks to a sluggish economic recovery from the Great Recession and backlash against the passage of the Affordable Care Act, Republicans took control of the House with a 63-seat gain – the largest House sweep since the 1940s – and won six seats in the Senate. But the 2010 midterms were significant well beyond those numbers. It was the first election shaped by the rise of the Tea Party and its blend of rightwing economic populism and xenophobia. Those aligned with the movement lost nearly twice the number of races they won, but the presence of an energized hard-right contingent among Republicans in Congress shaped legislative outcomes for the remainder of Obama’s term and beyond.

description: Telling people to set aside food, water and cash is all very well, but we need a truly joined-up resilience strategy – and we don’t have one Jean Coussins is chair of the House of Lords national resilience committee The public has been stocking up on bottled water, tinned food and wind-up radios since the government launched its Be Ready campaign last month. But it’s not the public’s willingness to prepare that should worry us. What’s missing is the government’s willingness to provide candid information about the escalating nature and frequency of the threats we face, and a coherent resilience plan that can be activated from the top of government to local, community and household levels. In July, the then security minister, Angela Eagle, admitted to the House of Lords national resilience committee, of which I am chair, that the government did not want to “ frighten people ”. description: Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks The Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34. While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “ it’s make or bake time ”. With the latest analysis pointing to heating of 2.7C by the end of the century – far beyond the 1.5C target in the Paris agreement – governments face another crunch moment: by pivoting away from fossil fuels, they can still avert the most dangerous impacts. Yet the UK’s Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to make the trip to Turkey; the French and German leaders chose to attend an EU summit in Dublin instead.

title: The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own | Editorial
author: Editorial
categories: Civil service | Politics | AI (artificial intelligence) | Class issues | Schools | Education | Universities | Higher education | UK news
description: Whitehall needs to change, but more technology isn’t enough. Opening routes to leadership would bring skills that are too often overlooked The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “ reactive and risk-averse ” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?” This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. To improve, Dame Antonia says the civil service must embrace AI. The efficacy of public service, she claimed, no longer has to be constrained by the limits of “ human bandwidth ”. That is an extraordinary claim. Technology can help speed up identifying someone at risk of homelessness – but it does not supply a home. Better administration and adequate resources need each other.

description: Nearly 2 million children are housed in dire conditions, anxious families are living out of carrier bags. There’s little sign of the hope our PM promised Two days after the Christmas of 2024, Andy Burnham put up a post on X that linked to a piece about housing in the Guardian. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, who was beginning to find his voice as a frank critic of Keir Starmer’s new government, did not mess about: “The Government should make building hundreds of thousands of council homes its defining purpose,” he said. “No other policy, achievable within a parliament, would have greater social and economic benefits.” In his first Labour conference speech as party leader and prime minister, Burnham reprised much the same argument, promising “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar era”. But by that point, he had also served notice that his commitment to a thoroughgoing council house revival might not be quite as cast iron as it seemed. The previous month, having insisted that all of the £39bn Rachel Reeves had promised to spend on the Starmer government’s Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) until 2036 should go on homes for social rent, he made something of a brazen U-turn , announcing that the allocation of the first £10bn would reflect the existing social homes target of 60%. But this was leavened with another bit of old-time Labour religion : “Councils built this country out of a housing crisis once before.
